    #Tutorial 1 (Laplace Transform)

    #Question 1

    Expressing in partial fractions,

    F(s)=s(s+1)10​=sA​+s+1B​

    Using Heaviside theorem,

    A=[s+110​]s=0​=10

    B=[s10​]s=−1​=−10

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    F(s)=s10​−s+110​

    f(t)=10−10e−t

    Let t→∞.

    t→∞lim​f(t)=f(∞)=10

    Using final value theorem,

    s→0lim​sF(s)=s→0lim​s+110​=10

    Final value theorem allows us to relate the steady-state behavior of f(t)
    to the behavior of     sF(s). If f(t) and dtdf(t)​ are Laplace transformable
    and if     t→∞lim​f(t) exists, then t→∞lim​f(t)=s→0lim​sF(s).

    #Question 2

    t→0+lim​f(t)=s→∞lim​sF(s)

    f(0+)=s→∞lim​(s+2)2s​

    f(0+)=s→∞lim​s2+4s+4s​

    f(0+)=s→∞lim​2s+41​ (L’ Hopital’s Rule)

    f(0+)=0

    Using initial value theorem,

    t→0+lim​f′(t)=s→∞lim​sL{f′(t)}

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​sL{f′(0+)}

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​s⋅(s+2)2s​

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​(s+2)2s2​

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​s2+4s+4s2​ (L’ Hopital’s Rule)

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​2s+42s​ (L’ Hopital’s Rule)

    f′(0+)=s→∞lim​22​

    #Tutorial 2 (Transfer Functions)

    #Question 1

    Reference input signal only,

    R(s)C(s)​Ref​=1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)​

    CRef​(s)=1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)​R(s)

    Disturbance input signal only,

    D(s)C(s)​Dtb​=1+G(s)⋅H(s)⋅K(s)G(s)​

    CDtb​(s)=1+G(s)⋅H(s)⋅K(s)G(s)​D(s)

    Note that the output of H(s) passes through a negative junction.
    Thus, it is a negative feedback loop (”+” in denominator).

    Noise input signal only,

    Cnoise​(s)=1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)−G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)​N(s)

    Algebraic computation,

    (N+Cnoise​)(−HKG)=Cnoise​

    −NHKG−Cnoise​HKG=Cnoise​

    −NHKG=Cnoise​(1+HKG)

    Cnoise​=1+HKG−NHKG​

    Note that the output of H(s) passes through a negative junction.
    Thus, we need to multiply by a negative sign for the numerator.

    Output signal of system,

    C(s)=CRef​(s)+CDtb​(s)+Cnoise​(s)

    C(s)=1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)⋅R(s)​+0+0

    C(s)=1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)​R(s)

    Error is the difference between input and output signals.

    E(s)=R(s)−B(s)

    E(s)=R(s)−C(s)

    E(s)=R(s)−1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)​R(s)

    E(s)=R(s)⋅[1−1+G(s)⋅K(s)⋅H(s)G(s)⋅K(s)​]

    E(s)=R(s)⋅[1−1+G(s)⋅KG(s)⋅K​]

    E(s)=R(s)⋅[1+G(s)⋅K1+G(s)⋅K−G(s)⋅K​]

    E(s)=1+G(s)⋅KR(s)​

    #Part (d)

    • Shift the branch between G1​ and G2​ to after G2​
    • Insert the function G2​1​ in the upper feedback loop
    • Obtain a closed-loop transfer function for G1​ and G2​
    • Obtain a closed-loop transfer function for the new diagram

    1st closed-loop transfer function,

    T.F.=1+G1​G2​G1​G2​​

    Note that H(s)=1.

    2nd closed-loop transfer function,

    T.F.=1−G(s)⋅H(s)G(s)​

    T.F.=1+G1​G2​G1​G2​​⋅1+G1​G2​−G1​1+G1​G2​​

    T.F.=1+G1​G2​−G1​G1​G2​​

    To compute the 2nd transfer function, let G(s)=1+G1​G2​G1​G2​​ and H(s)=G2​1​.

    Since feedback signal is added to the input signal, denominator has “-” sign.

    Compute the denominator of the transfer function,

    1−G(s)⋅H(s)=1−1+G1​G2​G1​​=1+G1​G2​1+G1​G2​−G1​​

    #Question 3

    Step 1
    • Swap the positions of the 2nd and 3rd junctions
    • Shift the branch before G2​ to after G2​
    • Divide the function H1​ by G2​

    Step 2
    • Replace the closed-loops with corresponding transfer functions
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation to G2​ and H2​
    • Perform algebraic computation for G2​H1​​

    Computing for the closed loop containing G2​H1​​,
    where     X is the input and Y is the output,

    X+X⋅G2​H1​​=Y

    X(1+G2​H1​​)=Y

    XY​=1+G2​H1​​

    Step 3
    • Compute G(s) for the closed-loop
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation

    Numerator of the equation,

    G(s)=1+G2​H2​G2​​(G2​H1​​+1)G3​

    G(s)=1+G2​H2​G2​G3​​⋅G2​H1​+G2​​

    G(s)=1+G2​H2​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    Denominator of the equation,

    1+G(s)⋅H(s)=1+1+G2​H2​G3​(H1​+G2​)​H3​

    1+G(s)⋅H(s)=1+G2​H2​1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)​

    Substituting into the equation,

    T.F.=1+G(s)⋅H(s)G(s)​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​G3​(H1​+G2​)​⋅1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)1+G2​H2​​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    Step 4
    • Compute G(s) for the closed-loop
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation

    Numerator of the equation,

    G(s)=1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    Denominator of the equation,

    1+G(s)=1+1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    1+G(s)=1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)+G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    1+G(s)=1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)1+G2​H2​+G3​(H1​+G2​)(H3​+G1​)​

    Note that H(s)=1.

    Substituting into the equation,

    T.F.=1+G(s)⋅H(s)G(s)​=1+G(s)G(s)​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​⋅1+G2​H2​+G3​(H1​+G2​)(H3​+G1​)1+G2​H2​+G3​H3​(H1​+G2​)​

    T.F.=1+G2​H2​+G3​(H1​+G2​)(H3​+G1​)G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    Transfer function of the block diagram is,

    T.F.=R(s)C(s)​=1+G2​H2​+G3​(H1​+G2​)(H3​+G1​)G1​G3​(H1​+G2​)​

    #Question 4

    Step 1
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation

    Transfer function is,

    T.F.=1+a1​/s1/s​

    T.F.=s1​⋅s+a1​s​

    T.F.=s+a1​1​

    Step 2
    • Shift b2​ junction ahead of of previous transfer function
    • Divide function b2​ by the previous transfer function

    Function b2​ changes to,

    1/(s+a1​)b2​​=b2​(s+a1​)

    Step 3
    • Swap b2​ junction with the other junctions
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation

    Note that consecutive summing junctions are swappable.

    G(s)=s2+a1​s1​

    G(s)⋅H(s)=s2+a1​sa2​​

    Transfer function is,

    T.F.=1+G(s)⋅H(s)G(s)​

    T.F.=s2+a1​s1​⋅s2+a1​s+a2​s2+a1​s​

    T.F.=s2+a1​s+a2​1​

    Step 4
    • Shift b1​ junction ahead of previous transfer function
    • Divide function b1​ by the previous transfer function

    Function b1​ changes to,

    b1​(s2+a1​s+a2​)

    Step 5
    • Apply closed-loop transfer function equation

    G(s)=s3+a1​s2+a2​s1​

    G(s)⋅H(s)=s3+a1​s2+a2​sa3​​

    Transfer function is,

    T.F.=s3+a1​s2+a2​s+a3​1​

    Step 6
    • Combine summing junctions into one function
    • Transfer function is then the product of the two functions

    Transfer function of the block diagram is,

    T.F.=R(s)Y(s)​=s3+a1​s2+a2​s+a3​b3​+b2​(s+a1​)+b1​(s2+a1​s+a2​)​

    #Tutorial 3 (Dynamic System Modelling)

    #Question 1

    Applying Newton’s 2nd law,

    mx¨=∑F

    mx¨=F−x˙(c1​+c2​)−x(k1​+k2​)

    F=mx¨+x˙(c1​+c2​)+x(k1​+k2​)

    Laplace transform of derivatives,

    L{x¨}=s2X(s)−sx(0)−x˙(0)

    L{x˙}=sX(s)−x(0)

    L{x}=X(s)

    Note that initial conditions are assumed to be zero.

    Performing Laplace transform,

    F(s)=m⋅s2X(s)+(c1​+c2​)⋅sX(s)+(k1​+k2​)⋅X(s)

    F(s)=X(s)[ms2+(c1​+c2​)s+(k1​+k2​)]

    Transfer function of the system is,

    InputOutput​=F(s)X(s)​=ms2+(c1​+c2​)s+(k1​+k2​)1​

    #Question 2

    Assume x>y. Spring is stretched.
    Thus, the spring force acts upwards.

    Applying Newton’s 2nd law,

    mx¨=∑F

    mx¨=−k(x−y)

    mx¨+kx=ky

    Force is negative as it acts in the opposite
    direction to positive displacement of output.

    Performing Laplace transform,

    m⋅s2X(s)+k⋅X(s)=k⋅Y(s)

    X(s)[ms2+k]=k⋅Y(s)

    Transfer function of the system is,

    InputOutput​=Y(s)X(s)​=ms2+kk​

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Using Newton’s 2nd law,

    Jθ¨=∑T

    Jθ¨=τ−Bθ˙

    τ=Jθ¨+Bθ˙

    Expressing in terms of angular velocity,

    τ=Jω˙+Bω

    Performing Laplace transform,

    T(s)=J⋅sΩ(s)+B⋅Ω(s)

    T(s)=(Js+B)⋅Ω(s)

    T(s)Ω(s)​=Js+B1​=100s+101​

    #Part (b)

    Laplace transform of input torque,

    L{100}=s100​

    Substituting into the transfer function,

    100/sΩ(s)​=100s+101​

    Ω(s)=100(s+0.1)1​⋅s100​

    Ω(s)=s(s+0.1)1​

    Ω(s)=s10​−s+0.110​

    Partial fractions of output,

    Ω(s)=s(s+0.1)1​=sA​+s+0.1B​

    A=[s+0.11​]s=0​=10

    B=[s1​]s=−0.1​=−10

    Performing inverse Laplace transform,

    ω(t)=10−10e−0.1t

    Steady-state value is obtained by letting t→∞.

    ω=10 rad/s

    R(s)C(s)​=s2+2s+22​

    #Part (b)

    From Tutorial 9 Exercise 1,

    R(s)C(s)​=1+(2s+2)/s2(2s+2)/s2​

    R(s)C(s)​=s2+2s+22s+2​

    Closed-loop transfer function (PD),

    R(s)C(s)​=s2+2s+22s+2​

    Closed-loop transfer function (PV),

    R(s)C(s)​=s2+2s+22​

    Since the numerator contains an “s” term for the PD controller, its transfer function is
    not a pure 2nd-order system. Thus, the response of the PD controller will be slower than the PV controller, which is a pure 2nd-order system.
